design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42018094623) of cohorts of people with regular, problematic or dependent use of amphetamines (methamphetamine and amphetamine together), pooling crude mortality rates per 100 person-years and standardised mortality ratios for all-cause death and for five causes: drug poisoning, accidental injury, suicide, homicide and cardiovascular disease. 30 eligible papers reporting 25 cohorts; 23 cohorts (115,223 people) contributed to the all-cause estimates. Standardised mortality ratios were imputed by the reviewers for 13 cohorts using Global Burden of Disease 2017 reference rates, and relative risks were derived from standardised mortality ratios by the Jones and Swerdlow correction.
can_establish: How often people in these cohorts died per unit of follow-up time, and how far that exceeds the death rate of age-, sex-, place- and period-matched general populations; which causes of death are most common and which are most elevated relative to the general population.
cannot_establish: That amphetamine use caused the excess deaths (cohorts are mostly clinical, treatment, prison or needle-exchange samples with heavy polysubstance use, and no cohort has a matched non-using comparison group); the risk attributable to methamphetamine as distinct from amphetamine, to dose, route or dependence severity; or the risk for people who use occasionally (cohorts required regular, problematic or dependent use).

sample.recruitment: Cohorts assembled from needle and syringe programmes, specialist drug treatment services, psychiatric and general hospital admissions, prison and criminal-justice samples, people apprehended for driving under the influence, HIV cohorts, injecting-drug-user cohorts and a conscript cohort, in North America, Nordic countries, Western and Central Europe, Australia, Taiwan and Thailand (Table 1). Cohort sizes ranged from 35 to 74,170 people (Table 1; the abstract and results text give the upper figure as 74,139), with total follow-up of about 752,292 person-years across the 25 cohorts (editors' sum of Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: cohort studies in which at least 90% of the sample reported use of amphetamines, or an identified amphetamine-using subgroup reported separately; case-control studies with mortality reported separately for cases defined by amphetamine use; trials of treatment for amphetamine use disorder reporting mortality at follow-up; secondary publications of included cohorts for methodological or baseline data. Excluded: case reports and series, non-original work, studies without obtainable mortality data, systematic reviews (hand-searched instead), studies not reporting use and mortality in the same people, studies where intentional use was unclear, trials of interventions for non-substance-use conditions, people recruited at the point of being prescribed stimulants or using them as prescribed, and cohorts of 30 or fewer people.
sample.demographics: Reporting was incomplete: fewer than half of the cohorts reported the proportion of women, 7 reported the proportion who injected, and HIV and HCV status, mental health and homelessness or incarceration were reported by fewer still. Where given, mean baseline age ranged from about 28 to 37 years and the proportion of women from 0% to 55%.
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level; loss to follow-up within cohorts is not summarized, although 'completeness' was one of the nine quality criteria and the paper states every study scored the same on it (so it could not be entered into meta-regression).
sample.selection_effects: Cohorts are overwhelmingly clinical, treatment-seeking, incarcerated or injecting samples: people with the heaviest use and the most co-occurring disadvantage. The authors' own meta-regression shows city-level samples had substantially higher crude mortality than national samples, which they attribute to sites being chosen where problems were already identified. Coverage is confined to high-income countries (one upper-middle-income cohort), leaving out most of the world where amphetamine use is growing. Older cohorts probably involved different drugs (less crystalline methamphetamine) than recent ones, which the authors could not examine.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each cohort used: self-reported injecting or use, treatment admission for amphetamine problems, hospital or registry diagnoses of amphetamine-related disorders, police detection of driving under the influence, or criminal-justice records. The review states the definition of problematic or dependent use varied across cohorts and summarizes each in Table 1; it names this variability as a likely source of the heterogeneity.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable. The review required regular, problematic or dependent use but did not pool by dose, frequency or dependence severity. Injecting status was reported by only 7 cohorts (0% to 100% of samples) and there were too few studies to test whether injecting predicted mortality.
exposure.polysubstance: Extensive and not adjustable: cohorts include people using opioids and other drugs, and several are general drug-treatment or injecting-drug-user cohorts with an amphetamine-using subgroup. The authors state that mortality was not reported in a way that allowed patterns of polydrug use or psychiatric comorbidity to be examined, and name this as a limitation.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: the outcome is death during follow-up, and use status after baseline was generally not measured.

comparison.controls: No internal comparison group in most cohorts. The comparator for standardised mortality ratios is the general population of the same age, sex, country and period, taken from Global Burden of Disease 2017 estimates for the 13 cohorts whose ratios the reviewers imputed; the other 8 used the authors' own reference populations. Relative risks were derived from the standardised mortality ratios by correcting for the proportion of the general population that is itself exposed (Jones and Swerdlow).
comparison.matching: Standardisation on age, sex, country and calendar period only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Everything that distinguishes people in these cohorts from the general population other than age and sex: socio-economic position, homelessness, incarceration, injecting, hepatitis C and HIV, other drug use, psychiatric illness and premorbid physical health. None of these is adjusted for, so the standardised mortality ratios measure the mortality of a severely disadvantaged population, not the effect of amphetamines.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The general-population comparator includes people who use drugs, which, as the authors note via the Jones and Swerdlow correction, makes standardised mortality ratios slightly conservative relative to a truly unexposed comparator.

outcomes.instruments: Death ascertained from national death registers, coronial records or cohort follow-up, as reported by each primary study. Causes were grouped to a published toolkit for classifying major causes of death among people who use illicit drugs. The authors state that in many studies it was not clear how cause of death was ascertained (coronial files or ICD coding, and which codes), and call this a limitation.
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study quality was scored with a bespoke 9-criterion index carried over from the team's earlier review (case ascertainment 0 to 3, measurement 0 to 2, diagnosis 0 to 2, estimate 0 to 1, numerator and denominator 0 to 1, data catchment 0 to 1, completeness 0 to 2, representativeness 0 to 2, age and sex variables 0 to 2; maximum 16). Scores in Table 1 range from 6 to 16, with most between 7 and 13. This is a quality index, not a validated risk-of-bias instrument, and no domain-level judgments are reported per study.
outcomes.operationalization: Two measures: crude mortality rate per 100 person-years (deaths divided by person-years of follow-up, with person-years approximated where unreported by assuming deaths occurred halfway through follow-up) and standardised mortality ratio (cohort rate divided by the matched general-population rate). Heterogeneity was labelled low (25% or less), moderate (above 25% to 50%) or substantial (75% or more).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 24 counts the 12 pooled crude mortality rates and 12 pooled standardised mortality ratios in Table 2 (all-cause, women, men, six regions, and five causes); further subgroup, sensitivity, relative-risk and meta-regression analyses are reported in the text and appendices.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles and abstracts were screened by one reviewer with a second checking the exclusions; full texts were screened by two independent reviewers with a third resolving disagreements; extraction and quality scoring were done by one reviewer and checked by a second.

analysis.effect_sizes: DerSimonian-Laird Mantel-Haenszel random-effects pooling in Stata 15.1 with I-squared; no tau-squared and no prediction intervals. All-cause: crude mortality rate 1.11 per 100 person-years (95% CI 0.90 to 1.37), 23 cohorts, I2=96.9%; standardised mortality ratio 6.83 (5.27 to 8.84), same 23 cohorts, I2=98.0%. By sex: crude rate 0.56 (0.40 to 0.77) in women (7 cohorts) and 0.97 (0.76 to 1.24) in men (10 cohorts); standardised ratio 5.91 (3.74 to 9.35) in women and 4.68 (3.43 to 6.40) in men; pooled within-study relative risk between sexes 2.10 (1.77 to 2.49). Cause-specific crude rates per 100 person-years: drug poisoning 0.14 (0.06 to 0.34), 5 cohorts, I2=95.5%; accidental injury 0.20 (0.08 to 0.47), 7 cohorts, I2=98.4%; suicide 0.20 (0.07 to 0.55), 6 cohorts, I2=98.2%; cardiovascular disease 0.13 (0.06 to 0.29), 4 cohorts, I2=94.2%; homicide 0.03 (0.02 to 0.06), 4 cohorts, I2=45.2%. Cause-specific standardised mortality ratios: drug poisoning 24.70 (16.67 to 36.58), I2=75.3%; suicide 12.20 (4.89 to 30.47), I2=97.7%; homicide 11.90 (7.82 to 18.12), I2=13.6%; cardiovascular disease 5.12 (3.74 to 7.00), I2=54.9%; accidental injury 5.12 (2.88 to 9.08), I2=95.5%. Regional all-cause standardised ratios ranged from 4.48 (East Asia) to 10.52 (Australasia) and did not differ significantly. Absolute framing (editors' calculation from the pooled rate): 1.11 deaths per 100 person-years is about 1,110 deaths per 100,000 person-years, that is roughly 1 death per 90 people per year of follow-up.
analysis.covariates: None at participant level. Study-level meta-regressions tested percentage women, region, country income, year of final follow-up, sampling frame, case ascertainment, representativeness and completeness.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42018094623; PRISMA and GATHER checklists in the appendix. No deviations from the registered protocol are described in the paper; the registration itself was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The paper is unusually explicit about what it could not do (age-specific rates, polydrug and comorbidity patterns, injecting status). Causes of death other than the five chosen are relegated to an appendix. Relative-risk results are reported only as being similar to the standardised mortality ratios, with the numbers in appendices. The sensitivity analysis quotes a pooled all-cause standardised mortality ratio for all 23 cohorts (6.08) that differs from the headline figure (6.83).
analysis.power: Not applicable in the usual sense, but several pooled estimates rest on very few cohorts (4 to 7 for each cause of death; 1 to 2 for several regions), and heterogeneity of 95% or more for most estimates means the pooled value describes no particular population. The authors state there were too few studies to examine age, HIV status or injecting.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 23 cohorts of people with regular, problematic or dependent amphetamine use, drawn mostly from treatment, hospital, prison and injecting populations in high-income countries, about 1.1 deaths occurred per 100 person-years of follow-up, roughly 6.8 times the rate expected for matched general populations. Deaths from drug poisoning were about 25 times, homicide about 12 times, suicide about 12 times, and cardiovascular disease and accidental injury about 5 times the expected rates. Heterogeneity was extreme for nearly every pooled estimate (I2 95% or more for all-cause and most cause-specific rates), and the only study-level variable that explained any of it was whether the sample was drawn from a city rather than nationally.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that people with regular or dependent amphetamine use are at elevated risk of a range of causes of mortality compared with people without such use. The discussion goes further: that interventions addressing amphetamine use disorders may reduce not only overdose but also other deaths "that appear to be causally related to use", and compares the elevation with that for opioid dependence. Gaps: (1) the causal reading is not supported by the design, since no cohort has a non-using comparison group and the comparator is the general population, so the excess includes everything that distinguishes these populations (poverty, injecting, imprisonment, polydrug use, psychiatric illness, hepatitis C, HIV); (2) the pooled estimates carry heterogeneity of 96 to 98% and no prediction interval, so a single number is close to uninterpretable as a risk for any one population; (3) the headline multiplier appears in the paper as 6.83, 6.3 and 6.2 in different places; (4) the comparison with the opioid figure of about 14-fold comes from a different review with different cohorts; (5) the conclusion is about amphetamines in general, while the cohorts span decades in which the drug supply changed from amphetamine to crystalline methamphetamine, a limitation the authors state but the conclusion does not carry.

timeline.event: Singleton, Degenhardt, Hall and Zabransky: earlier systematic review of mortality in people who use amphetamines, 8 cohorts published 1980 to 2007; this review used it as the source for pre-2008 studies.
This review: 25 cohorts, about 752,000 person-years, first pooled cause-specific estimates.
Companion meta-analysis from an overlapping author group on mental-health outcomes of amphetamine use

replication.where_it_stands: The largest synthesis of mortality in this population and the only one with cause-specific pooled estimates. It supersedes the 2009 review by the same group and incorporates it, so the two are not independent. Primary cohorts inside it overlap with studies the encyclopedia may cite separately (for example Callaghan's Californian hospital cohorts), so claims must not treat them as independent support.

funding.funder: NHMRC Research Fellowships (GNT1041742, GNT1135991, GNT1091878, GNT1140938, 1104600, 1109366) and NIDA R01DA1104470 support individual authors; the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre at UNSW Sydney is funded by the Australian Government Department of Health under the Drug and Alcohol Program (Acknowledgements).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at NDARC, UNSW Sydney, except one at the University of Queensland. Several authors also authored the 2009 review that supplied the pre-2008 studies and set the quality index used here.

what_would_settle_it: Linkage cohorts that follow people identified as using amphetamines alongside a comparison group matched on socio-economic position, injecting status, other drug use and psychiatric history (for example sibling or matched-population designs in national registers), with cause of death coded to stated ICD rules and with exposure measured by drug, dose and route over time, would separate the mortality attributable to amphetamine use from the mortality of the populations in which it is concentrated.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (regular, problematic or dependent use), outcomes (all-cause and five specific causes) and comparator (general population) specified.
PROSPERO CRD42018094623 with PRISMA and GATHER checklists in the appendix; the registration itself was not read, so deviations cannot be checked.
Cohorts, case-control studies with mortality by exposure, and treatment trials, with explicit exclusions including cohorts of 30 or fewer.

Three databases via OVID with full strategies, no language restriction (non-English citations read via machine translation), reference lists of reviews hand-searched, journal contents searched, authors contacted for missing data, and the final list sent to experts. Weaknesses: the search covers 2008 to February 2018 and relies on the team's own earlier review for 1980 to 2007, and no grey literature or registry search is described.
Titles and abstracts screened by one reviewer with a second checking only the exclusions; full texts screened independently by two reviewers with a third for disagreements.
One extractor with a second checking, for both data and quality scoring.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Appendix G is stated to list the excluded studies; the appendix was not read, so whether reasons are given per study is unverified.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, years, quality score, sample description, n, person-years, percentage women, baseline age and percentage injecting, but many cells are blank, and the exposure definition per cohort is only summarized.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A 9-criterion quality index (maximum 16) carried over from the authors' earlier review, double-checked and used in meta-regression; but it is not a validated risk-of-bias instrument for cohort studies, confounding is not assessed as a domain, and only a summary score is reported per study.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling is the right family of model and the sensitivity analysis comparing author-reported with imputed standardised mortality ratios is a strength; but rates and ratios are pooled with I2 of 95 to 98% without tau-squared or prediction intervals, 13 of 23 standardised mortality ratios are reviewer-imputed against Global Burden of Disease reference rates, and several pooled cells contain one or two cohorts.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Meta-regressions on case ascertainment, representativeness and completeness, plus sensitivity analyses removing the HIV cohort and restricting to author-reported standardised mortality ratios.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations section is thorough about cohort assembly, cause-of-death coding and changing drug supply, but the discussion still describes several causes of death as appearing causally related to use, which the design cannot support.

I2 reported for every estimate, subgroup and meta-regression analyses run, and the one significant finding (city versus national sampling frame) interpreted; most heterogeneity remains unexplained and the paper says so.
Funnel plots and an analysis of the association between cohort size and estimates, reported in Appendix J as showing no evidence of bias; the appendix was not read.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding listed and no conflicts declared; the paper does not note that the authors also wrote the earlier review that supplied the pre-2008 studies and the quality index.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical AMSTAR 2 item is failed outright: the review is registered, the search is broad and multilingual, publication bias was examined, and the impact of study quality was tested. Confidence is held at low because four critical items are only partially met: the excluded-study list and the publication-bias analysis sit in unread appendices, the appraisal instrument is a bespoke summary quality score rather than a risk-of-bias tool with domains (confounding in particular is never assessed), and the pooled estimates carry 95 to 98% heterogeneity with no prediction intervals while 13 of 23 standardised mortality ratios were imputed by the reviewers. If item 9 were scored as a failure on the ground that a summary quality index is not a risk-of-bias assessment, the rating would fall to critically low. Separately from AMSTAR 2: the standardised mortality ratios compare a severely disadvantaged population with the general population without adjustment, so they measure excess mortality in these cohorts and not the mortality effect of amphetamines.

key_findings.finding: Of 4,240 unique papers, 101 were screened in full text and 30 were included, reporting 25 cohorts followed for about 752,292 person-years (editors' sum of Table 1; the discussion says more than 750,000). Cohort size ranged from 35 to 74,170 people.
key_findings.note: The abstract and results text give the largest cohort as 74,139 while Table 1 gives 74,170.

key_findings.finding: Pooled all-cause crude mortality rate across 23 cohorts (115,223 people): 1.11 deaths per 100 person-years (95% CI 0.90 to 1.37), I2=96.9%. Editors' calculation: about 1,110 deaths per 100,000 person-years.
key_findings.locator: Results › Crude mortality rates, 1st paragraph; Table 2, all-cause row

key_findings.finding: Pooled all-cause standardised mortality ratio across the same 23 cohorts: 6.83 (95% CI 5.27 to 8.84), I2=98.0%. Eight cohorts reported their own ratios; the reviewers imputed ratios for 13 cohorts using Global Burden of Disease 2017 reference rates.
key_findings.locator: Results › Standardised mortality ratios, 1st paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: The discussion restates this elevation as 6.3-fold and, later, 6.2-fold; the sensitivity analysis gives 6.08 (4.41 to 8.37) for the same 23 cohorts.

key_findings.finding: Cause-specific crude mortality rates per 100 person-years: drug poisoning 0.14 (0.06 to 0.34), 5 cohorts; accidental injury 0.20 (0.08 to 0.47), 7 cohorts; suicide 0.20 (0.07 to 0.55), 6 cohorts; cardiovascular disease 0.13 (0.06 to 0.29), 4 cohorts; homicide 0.03 (0.02 to 0.06), 4 cohorts. Heterogeneity was 94 to 98% for all except homicide (45.2%).
key_findings.note: The abstract prints the cardiovascular interval as 0.06 to 0.55, which matches the suicide row rather than Table 2's cardiovascular row (0.06 to 0.29).

key_findings.finding: Cause-specific standardised mortality ratios: drug poisoning 24.70 (16.67 to 36.58), I2=75.3%; suicide 12.20 (4.89 to 30.47), I2=97.7%; homicide 11.90 (7.82 to 18.12), I2=13.6%; cardiovascular disease 5.12 (3.74 to 7.00), I2=54.9%; accidental injury 5.12 (2.88 to 9.08), I2=95.5%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, cause-specific rows; Results › Standardised mortality ratios, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: By sex: pooled crude mortality rate 0.56 per 100 person-years (0.40 to 0.77) in women (7 cohorts, 44,580 people) and 0.97 (0.76 to 1.24) in men (10 cohorts, 42,248 people); standardised mortality ratio 5.91 (3.74 to 9.35) in women and 4.68 (3.43 to 6.40) in men. The pooled within-study relative risk between the sexes was 2.10 (1.77 to 2.49).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, women and men rows; Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The results text labels this relative risk 'women vs. men' while the discussion reads it as men having 2.1 times the risk of women; the crude rates support the latter direction. The standardised ratios go the other way (higher in women) because female general-population mortality is lower.

key_findings.finding: Regional all-cause standardised mortality ratios did not differ significantly: Australasia 10.52 (9.30 to 11.89, 2 cohorts, I2=0%), Western Europe 7.81 (5.03 to 12.12, 11 cohorts), Southeast Asia 7.30 (0.82 to 65.30, 2 cohorts), Central Europe 6.22 (4.64 to 8.34, 1 cohort), high-income North America 5.09 (3.55 to 7.30), East Asia 4.48 (2.53 to 7.93).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, GBD region rows; Results › Standardised mortality ratios, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Meta-regression found no association of percentage women, year of study, region, country income or methodological quality variables with crude or standardised mortality. The one significant result was sampling frame: city-level cohorts had higher crude mortality than national cohorts (coefficient 3.249, SE 0.813, p<0.001; adjusted R-squared 61.25% for the crude-rate model), an association not seen for standardised ratios (p=0.085). Case ascertainment was associated with crude mortality (coefficient 0.748, SE 0.076, p=0.010) but not standardised ratios.
key_findings.locator: Results › Factors associated with CMR and SMR; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: restricting to the 8 cohorts whose authors reported their own standardised mortality ratios gave 5.71 (4.44 to 7.35), close to the pooled value; removing the single HIV-positive cohort gave a crude rate of 1.09 (0.97 to 1.22) and a standardised ratio of 6.47 (4.96 to 8.43). Funnel plots and an analysis of cohort size versus estimates (Appendix J) showed no evidence of publication bias.

Study quality scores (bespoke 9-criterion index, maximum 16) ranged from 6 to 16 across the 25 cohorts, with most between 7 and 13; the index measures case ascertainment, measurement, diagnosis, estimate, numerator and denominator, data catchment, completeness, representativeness and age/sex variables, and is not a risk-of-bias instrument.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data extraction, last paragraph; Table 1, quality score column

key_findings.finding: The authors compare the elevation in this population (stated in the discussion as about 6.2-fold) with an approximately 14-fold elevation reported for people with opioid dependence in a different review.
key_findings.note: Cross-review comparison between different cohorts and periods, not a within-study comparison.

key_findings.finding: Reporting limits named by the authors: cause-of-death ascertainment was often unclear (coronial files versus ICD codes unspecified), age-specific rates were rarely reported, and polydrug use and psychiatric comorbidity could not be examined; older cohorts probably involved amphetamine rather than crystalline methamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the pooled cardiovascular crude mortality rate as 0.13 per 100 person-years (95% CI 0.06 to 0.55); Table 2 gives 0.13 (0.06 to 0.29). The abstract's upper limit duplicates the suicide row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any claim citing the cardiovascular rate must use the Table 2 interval; the abstract overstates the imprecision.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline all-cause elevation appears as 6.83 (abstract and Table 2), 6.3-fold (discussion, 1st paragraph), 6.2-fold (discussion, 2nd paragraph) and 6.08 (sensitivity analysis, described as the pooled estimate for the same 23 studies).
reporting_issues.consequence: Four values for one estimate. The table value of 6.83 (5.27 to 8.84) should be cited; the 6.08 figure in the sensitivity section is unexplained and may come from a differently specified model.

reporting_issues.issue: The list of cohorts contributing to the all-cause estimates differs between the results text (references 17, 19 to 30, 34 to 43) and Table 2 (references 17 to 30, 34, 35, 37 to 39, 41 to 44): the text includes references 36 and 40 and omits 18 and 44, while the table does the opposite.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which cohorts are in the pooled estimate cannot be determined from the paper; the regional totals in Table 2 fit the table's list, so the text's list appears to be the erroneous one.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 describes Callaghan 2013 (reference 36, a motor-vehicle-accident mortality study, n=74,170) but not Callaghan 2012 (reference 18), which Table 2 lists as contributing to the all-cause, women's, men's, accidental-injury and North American estimates.
reporting_issues.consequence: A cohort contributing to several pooled estimates, and apparently the largest in the North American group, is not described in the table of included studies, so its sample, follow-up and quality cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 reference lists are shorter than the stated study counts: the men's row gives 8 references for 10 studies, high-income North America gives 4 references for 5 studies, and Western Europe gives 9 references for 11 studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled sets cannot be reconstructed; the participant totals are internally consistent (the regional counts sum to the all-cause total of 115,223), so the counts rather than the reference lists appear correct.

reporting_issues.issue: The Southeast Asia row reports 769 people in 2 cohorts (references 26 and 41), but Table 1 gives those cohorts as 320 and 1,116 people, totalling 1,436.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a subgroup of each cohort was used or the figure is wrong; the regional estimate (crude rate 2.02, 95% CI 0.23 to 17.98) is in any case too imprecise to support a claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The sex-specific analysis is described in the results as giving a relative risk of 2.10 'for women vs. men' and in the discussion as men having 2.1 times the risk of women; the two sex-specific crude rates (0.56 in women, 0.97 in men) imply a ratio of about 1.7 in the direction stated in the discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the sex difference is stated inconsistently, and the pooled within-study relative risk does not match the ratio of the pooled rates (different sets of cohorts, 7 and 10).

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that 9 studies (86,942 people) provided sex-specific standardised mortality ratios, while Table 2 reports 7 studies for women (44,580) and 10 for men (42,248), summing to 86,828.
reporting_issues.consequence: Study counts and participant totals for the sex-specific analyses do not reconcile across the text and the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The heterogeneity categories defined in the methods (low 25% or less, moderate above 25% to 50%, substantial 75% or more) leave the band above 50% and below 75% unnamed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the cardiovascular standardised ratio (I2=54.9%) falls in the undefined band.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction contains a stray character: the aim refers to conditions 'w4hich might be casually related' to amphetamine use, where 'causally' is meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical only, but the sentence is the paper's statement of causal intent and should be quoted carefully.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6732053 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1, 2 and 3 rendered as text, acknowledgements and conflict statement read; Figures 1 to 3, including the PRISMA flowchart and all forest plots, are images and their values were not extracted; Appendices A to J, including the excluded-study list, relative-risk estimates and publication-bias analyses, were not read)
